newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss economy worse than thought last year-experts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss economy worse than thought last year-experts.

text.p: Switzerland on Tuesday revised downward its 1995 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data to show virtual stagnation in 1995, but economists do not think the new numbers are cause for more revisions of estimates for this year and next.
Swiss GDP rose at an annual rate of 0.1 percent last year, according to figures released today by the Federal Statistics office.
The earlier provisional report showed a 1995 growth rate of 0.7 percent.
"There will be a basis effect, but our forecast for a zero figure (for 1996) is already optimistic," Thomas Heller at Credit Suisse said.
Credit Suisse expects modest 1997 growth of 0.6 percent.
Economists at Union Bank of Switzerland agree the data do not mean that their outlook for 1996 and 1997 must change.
"First of all we had expected that the numbers would be revised downward," UBS economist Alexander Kobler said.
He also said the main revision to last year's figures had to do with fourth quarter data.
Although the new number makes for a more favourable basis effect, it will be somewhat neutralised by the methods used to calculate year-on-year changes, he added.

Bank Julius Baer economist Hans Kaufmann said the bank had recently made another revision of its 1996 forecast. Although the new statistics office numbers might lead to the adjustment of some components, he agreed the overall forecast should remain unchanged.

Baer is forecasting a 1996 GDP contraction of a full 1.0 percent, down from a July estimate of zero growth. Its forecast for 1997 was revised down to a 0.7 percent growth rate from an earlier 1.2 percent.
The economy stagnated last year as the stimulating effect of domestic demand was neutralised by a worsening balance in trade and services, the office said in its report.
Swiss National Bank chief economist Georg Rich said on Monday he did not expect the Swiss economy to show any sustained expansion until 1997.
But the new data give little hope for any dramatic reversal of the country's stalled economy.

The final 1995 GDP figures showed that the export of trade and services grew by a nominal 0.1 percent while private consumption grew by 2.5 percent and overall domestic demand was up by a nominal 3.3 percent.
The Statistics office also reported on Tuesday retail sales fell by 0.4 percent in July after a year-on-year decline of 3.0 percent in June.
The GDP revision was also due in large degree to a drastic change in the construction spending figures, a statistics office economist said.
"They greatly overestimated construction spending," said Credit Suisse's Heller.

Figures based on fourth quarter estimates put the decline in construction spending at a nominal 1.4 percent. But revised figures showed a decline in building spending of 4.4 percent, statistics office economist Rolf Bayalar said.
Last month BAK, one of Switzerland's leading economic research institutes, said it revised downward its 1996 forecast to a contraction of 0.4 percent from the earlier forecast of 0.9 percent growth.
It said the revision was due to continued weak consumption, the half-hearted depreciation of the Swiss franc and the lack of stimulus from key trading partners.
